segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now the Spirit says explicitly that in later times some will turn away from the faith, devoting themselves to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: through the hypocrisy of liars whose own conscience has been seared,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who forbid marriage and demand abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and have come to know the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for it is made holy through God’s word and prayer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If you lay these things before the brothers and sisters, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, nourished on the words of the faith and of the good teaching that you have followed closely.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But have nothing to do with profane old wives’ tales. Train yourself instead for godliness;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for training the body is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for everything, holding a promise of life, the present life and the life to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The saying is trustworthy and deserves full acceptance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this is why we toil and are reviled: because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Command these things and teach them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one look down on you because you are young, but set the believers an example in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading, to exhortation, to teaching.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of hands by the council of elders.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Practice these things; be absorbed in them, so that your progress may be plain to all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Keep watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in these things, for by doing so you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

notes.note: The verb means to burn with a hot iron. It may picture a conscience cauterized into numbness, or one branded with a mark of ownership, as slaves and criminals were, here implying ownership by the deceiving powers of verse 1. Most translations and commentators take the first sense, but the second is a serious possibility and cannot be excluded.

notes.traditional: the word of God and prayer
notes.note: It is unclear what 'God's word' refers to. It may be God's own declaration in Genesis that what he made is good, or scriptural words spoken in a grace at table, or the gospel message. The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

The Greek calls the stories 'profane and old-womanish'. The second word was a stock put-down in philosophical polemic for stories thought unworthy of belief. It is conventional sarcasm aimed at the content of the rival teaching, not a comment on who was spreading it.

The Greek phrase can mean 'to a small extent' or 'for a short time'. The contrast with 'for everything' favours extent, but the following mention of the present life and the life to come gives the time sense some support. The rendering keeps the Greek's deliberate parallel between 'a little' and 'everything'.

This translation normally renders the adjective 'faithful' or 'believing'. Here it describes a statement, not a person, and means that the saying can be relied on. 'A faithful saying' is no longer natural English, so 'trustworthy' is used for this formula.

This formula recurs in the letters to Timothy and Titus to mark a statement as established teaching. Here it is disputed whether it points back to the saying about godliness in verse 8 or forward to verse 10. Most interpreters take it as pointing back.

Manuscripts are divided between 'we are reviled' (the SBLGNT reading, followed here and by the King James tradition) and 'we struggle', which many modern editions and translations prefer. The two Greek words look and sound similar, and either could have given rise to the other.

The usual sense of the word is 'especially', which makes God the Savior of all people and of believers in a particular way. A minority of scholars argue it can mean 'that is to say', which would make 'those who believe' a definition of 'all people'. That sense is disputed, and the ordinary meaning is kept.
In a list of observable qualities the word could equally mean 'faithfulness', that is, reliability. Most translations keep 'faith', and the Greek does not settle the question.

The word means reading aloud to a gathering, as the Scriptures were read in the synagogue, not private study. Few people owned books, and most heard the Scriptures only when they were read aloud. The three activities named together look like the elements of a meeting: reading, exhortation based on it, and instruction.

The word names the elders of a community as a body. It is also used of the Jewish council in Jerusalem. Laying on of hands was the recognised gesture for commissioning someone to a task. 2 Timothy 1:6 speaks of Paul's own hands in connection with Timothy's gift, and how the two statements relate is not certain.

candidates.reason: It is a key term of the Pastoral letters, also found in Acts and 2 Peter, and 'godliness', 'piety', 'reverence' and 'devotion' are all defensible, so it needs one rendering throughout.
The plural addressed to mixed congregations recurs across every letter, and translators split between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'believers'.
It is frequent in the Pastoral letters and traditionally varies between 'doctrine', 'teaching' and 'instruction', which hides the repetition within and across chapters.
It recurs in Romans, 1 Corinthians, the Pastoral letters and 1 Peter, and translators vary between 'gift', 'spiritual gift' and 'grace-gift', as well as the loanword 'charism'.
It is used of both the Jerusalem council (Luke 22:66; Acts 22:5) and a church body, and it should be aligned with the rendering of πρεσβύτερος.
